fable.line: **Grade: C+.** The chapter skeleton, the construct inventory and almost every Effect API name are right for effect 4.1.0, but the text contradicts three dated VIP amendments (VIP-1's removal of `effect f()`, VIP-16's `let` binding, VIP-32's 4.1.0 pin), omits VIP-33's amendment while three examples violate it, writes an Effect TypeScript column that does not type-check as written (`Effect<A, E, R>`

opus.line: **Grade: C.** The structure is the best this language has had: 10 short chapters, one VIP per section, a mapping beside every construct. But it reinstates a syntax VIP-1 removed, in 27 of its examples. Its throw-tracking rule, read literally, makes almost every Effect call in its own examples a compile error. And four of its Effect TS mappings give a different `Exit` from the VibeLang they claim t

sol.line: C — The core is substantially simpler and most Effect mappings are valid, but missed accepted amendments and incomplete lowering rules prevent this from being an implementation-agreement specification.

astra.line: D — The specification captures the new language’s simpler structure, but misses accepted amendments and does not yet define an unambiguous, compositional Effect 4.1.0 translation.

fable.line: **Grade: A-.** All seven round-9 findings and the three nits are fixed in the graded tree, the 38 VIPs are byte-identical to round 9 so the spec has no new source to track, every Effect TypeScript mapping checks out against effect 4.1.0 (29 APIs present, the eleven-name clash list exact, the readonly/mutable schema types and the computed-key decoder behave as written), and the grammar now writes e

opus.line: **Grade: A-.** All 10 of my round-9 findings are fixed, and every Effect TS mapping I probed gives the stated `Exit` on effect 4.1.0. Two majors remain: the `provide` keyword trigger has two readings, and so does the scope of the `Function` ban.

sol.line: A — The specification faithfully states the settled VIP language, and this fresh review found no concrete specification defect outside the expressly excluded pending decisions.

astra.line: A — The specification faithfully states the settled VIP language, fixes both of my round-9 findings, and has one minor catch-chain wording issue with no identified incorrect settled Effect lowering.

fable.line: **Grade: A-.** All five round-10 minors and all four nits are fixed in the graded tree, the 38 VIPs are byte-identical to round 10, every Effect TypeScript mapping checks out against effect 4.1.0 (this round's probes add interruption past a `using`, `raceAll` failure order, empty race operands, type-literal computed keys, `Data.TaggedEnum<{}>`, `Context.Service.Shape` and the `Context.Reference` c

opus.line: **Grade: A-.** All six of my round-10 findings are fixed and every probed Effect TS mapping gives the stated `Exit` on effect 4.1.0, but two majors sit in the `!` type shorthand: an optional trailing `R` after `A!!` that swallows the next line or a function body, and a `!=`/`!==` split that breaks valid TypeScript after `as`.

sol.line: A — The specification accurately states the accepted VIP language, with no concrete defect found outside the expressly excluded pending decisions.

astra.line: A — The specification faithfully states the settled VIP decisions, fixes my sole round-10 finding, and has no new graded defects identified in this review.

fable.line: # Grade: C. The runtime semantics that are implemented are largely right, but the call rule of 2026-10-27/28 (D421, D445, D480, D483, D490, D495, EK4613, EK4410) is not implemented, the plain form is absent from declarations so a library consumer silently gets unrun Effects, and the release notes list neither gap.

opus.line: Grade: D. The compiler is careful wherever it implements the older call model (evaluation order, regions, hygiene, fibers, iterators, cleanup), but it silently drops Effects in ordinary code, grows exponentially on unannotated call chains until it runs out of memory, emits invalid declarations, and leaves most of D480-D497 and twelve registry diagnostics unimplemented and unlisted.

sol.line: D — Substantial working compiler and runtime machinery is present, but five newly demonstrated major defects prevent release against the normative specification.

v2.title: 'A function that returns an Effect can't throw' contradicts body inference for a plain .vibe function that returns an Effect
v2.origin_evidence: 003:40 bullet '- A function that returns an Effect can't throw: an `effect` function, … or a `.ts` function whose return type is `Effect`. A call of it is never throw-tracked' is a '+' line in `diff -u v1/opus/spec v2/opus/spec` (003-failures.md hunk @@ -24,19 +24,23 @@); v1 had only 'A `.vibe` function's thrown type is inferred from its body'. v1/FIXED.md: 'opus | B2 | a/c | Fixed: effectful func
lego_vips: VIP-4 body inference for plain .vibe functions
v2.circles_why: B2's fix keyed 'effectful' on the return type instead of the function kind, so a plain .vibe function that builds an Effect falls under both bullets.

v2.title: Completion records send an unlabeled break to the innermost loop; JS sends it to a switch (and labeled break to a labeled block)
v2.origin_evidence: 002:512 '- The records are `Normal`, … An unlabeled `break` or `continue` targets the innermost enclosing loop, as in JavaScript, and the record names that loop.' is a '+' line in `diff -u v1/opus/spec v2/opus/spec` (new section '### Leaving a block'). v1 had no lowering for jumps. v1/FIXED.md: 'opus | M6 | Fixed: completion-record translation for block jumps (spec-fix)', same fix for sol M3, astr
v2.circles_why: The fix copied the jump-target rule by hand and wrote 'loop' where JavaScript says 'iteration or switch statement' (and any labeled statement for labeled break).

v2.title: Fixed checks for Option/Exit/Result patterns have no inventory, no Effect TS, no resolution rule (and Option.Some is undefined in 4.1.0)
v2.origin_evidence: v1/opus/spec/004-match.md already says 'the compiler tests those types with fixed checks: `when Option.Some(let v):` compiles to a test of the value's tag' ('-' line at diff 004 hunk @@ -37,7 +54,7 @@); v2 only appended 'and binds its `value` field to `v`'. Earliest: v1. No v1 graded finding covers it; sol v1 mentioned the missing mapping only in its ungraded mapping table (v1/sol/REPORT.md:177).

v9.title: provide's 'providers and { on one line' is prose, not [no LineTerminator here]; a provider list or provider value that spans lines has two readings
v9.origin_evidence: Unchanged by diff v8→v9 (no hunk touches 005:112 or 900:258). 005 'Its providers and the block's `{` are on one line' is in v1–v9 (grep 'providers and the block'); the 900 production comment `(providers and "{" on one line)` is in v5–v9. v8 fable REPORT:139 and :148 restated the rule and its cost as ungraded design notes, not a finding.
v9.circles_why: v2 fixed the provider grammar's delimitation (ConditionalExpression providers, separator commas) but left the line restriction as a comment; v9 turned every other prose line rule into [no LineTerminator here] (fable: 15→1) and skipped provide.

v9.title: A field ends at any line break (900:404), but 'as between interface members' (900:339, 006:9) is TypeScript's greedy type-member rule; a Prettier-wrapped multi-line union or function type is a syntax error under one and a field under the other
v9.origin_evidence: Neither sentence changed v8→v9 (900 'Fields.' paragraph hunk at diff line 827 is context only). 'A field ends at `;`, `,`, a line break or `}`' and 'type-member separators' first appear in v4 (grep); 'as between interface members' in v2.
v9.circles_why: v4's fix for v3 opus m13 unified Field/Separator by adding LineTerminator as a separator, without saying the type is parsed greedily first, so it fixed one-line fields and broke multi-line types.

v9.title: The spec recommends `a catch ((e) => b) catch ((e) => c)` to chain, but its own rule says the outer catch needs an Effect operand, so the documented chain is a type error
v9.origin_evidence: v8 002 already had both sentences: 'Parenthesize the arrow to chain: `a catch ((e) => b) catch c`' and 'In `(a catch b) catch c`, the outer `catch` runs the value … must itself be an Effect' (diff lines 170, 172). v9 only rewrote the handlers to function literals (decided detail 31a, diff lines 173, 176). Both sentences are in v2/opus/spec/002-running.md:81 and :83.
lego_vips: VIP-5 left-associative catch (amended) × VIP-5 catch runs its operand (yield* Effect.catch)
v9.circles_why: Each round fixed how the chain parses (parenthesized arrow, CatchHead trees, plain-arrow body) and never checked that the recommended chain type-checks against the 'must itself be an Effect' rule beside it; v1 sol and astra and v2–v5 opus flagged the typing cost only as ungraded notes.

v18.title: 002's array-default recipe `try { … } finally { if (!$done) $it.return?.() }` is not ECMAScript IteratorClose: a throwing `return()` replaces a pending throw (Die("close") vs native Die("body")), and a primitive `return()` result is ignored (Success(7) vs native Die(TypeError))
v18.origin_evidence: first.sh '$it.return?.()' => v18 only. v17/FIXED.md 'Integrator fixes beyond the lanes': '002: detail 68a stated once against ECMAScript's BindingInitialization, IteratorBindingInitialization and DestructuringAssignmentEvaluation: … IteratorClose in a `finally`', added after probe P5 ('array default with an abrupt completion: native calls `return()`; without `finally` the lowering skips it'). That
v18.circles_why: Every round re-lowers do/match in destructuring defaults by hand (IIFE in v17, statements plus finally in v18) instead of citing the ECMAScript algorithm; each hand recipe was probed only on the case that broke last time.

v18.title: The normative thrown-signature inventory `docs/design/inventory/throws.json` decides which calls compile but does not exist; 003 says it 'awaits its generator'
v18.origin_evidence: The defect predates v18: v17/ORIGINS.json row 'The generated Appendix E inventory … is still not published' labels it late-found v12 (Appendix E 'it, not this table, decides which calls compile'). The quoted 003 sentence is new (first.sh 'That artifact awaits its generator' and 'docs/design/inventory/throws.json' => v18 only), added by the round-17 sol M2 fix (v17/FIXED.md: 'name the normative `do
v18.circles_why: The round-17 fix gave the artifact a path and a schema but no contents, and v17/FIXED.md 'Integrator fixes' says it was written 'by path, not a link to a missing file (the docs link gate would fail)', so the gate that would have caught it was deliberately avoided.

v18.title: 004 Exhaustiveness: Subjects turns EK4701 off for any object type, but the Coverage parenthetical '(or an object member whose literal `_tag` is "V")' and the example `match (d) { when { _tag: "Sent", let tracking }: 1; } // EK4701` (d a plain object union) assume it runs
v18.origin_evidence: first.sh 'turns the check off for that', 'or an object member whose literal', 'Waiting not covered' => v17 v18; none appears in v16. All three entered v17 with detail 78 (decided-details.md:414, 'NW 42 and 46; … r16-004') and are unchanged in the r17→r18 diff. No round-17 reviewer reported it.
v18.circles_why: v15 opus M2 ('the trigger for EK4701, "a finite union", is undefined') was settled by detail 78, whose own example list kept an object-union subject the new Subjects rule excludes.

for_will.title: Round 8's 4 real circles: one area, no decision needed from you
for_will.due: Explanation only. The fix is in round 9
for_will.body:
All four repeats are the same area: VibeLang's declaration keywords `error`, `schema`, `service` and `data`. Elsewhere in TypeScript these words are ordinary names, as in `const data = …` or `service as {…}`. Each round patched one keyword's line-break rule:

```vibe
service as { a: string };   // TypeScript expression, or a service named `as`?
schema User
  = { id: string }          // is the lin
for_will.decided: Explanation only: round 9 applies the TypeScript `type` rule to all four keywords.

for_will.title: catch: is the handler always a function? (your question)
for_will.due: You accepted 2B; this is your follow-up idea
for_will.body:
Your idea: the handler is always a function literal, and its syntax says what it does.

```vibe
x catch (e) => fallback(e)        // plain function: its result is the value
x catch effect (e) => retry(e)    // effect function: runs, may fail again
x catch () => guest               // replaces 2B's value form `x catch guest`
x catch (e) => f(e)               // a named function is wrapped, so synta
for_will.decided: Your decision: the handler is always a function literal. `catch (e) => v` gives a value, `catch effect (e) => …` runs an Effect, and the value form is gone. Applied to the spec, VIP-5 and the compiler.
